title: Big and Small Hospitals
concept: Small samples vary more: a hospital with 15 births a day has more days with over 60% boys than one with 45 births a day, even though every baby is a 50/50 chance.
kept: The big hospital vs small hospital question about days with over 60% boys
The 'about the same' answer the friend is expected to give, offered as one of the guess options
Simulating a year of births in both hospitals and counting the days
Hospital theme with baby blue (boys) and pink (girls) colors, flat 2D
filled_in: Hospital sizes: 45 and 15 births a day (the standard classroom version of this problem)
Order: guess, run 1 day and count the dots, run the rest of the year, see the counts, press Why?, then explore
A 365-square year chart per hospital; dark squares mark days over 60% boys, and clicking a square shows that day's babies
Two-step explanation: the boys needed to pass 60% in each hospital, then how many above half that is, plus each hospital's lowest and highest day
Explore: a slider for the small hospital's size (5 to 45, steps of 5) and a 'Run a new year' button that adds a row to a results table
Model label: each baby is 50/50 and independent; same number of births every day

changed.what: The student's own belief that the answer is 'probably the same' is not used as the answer; the page shows the small hospital has more such days
changed.why: With fewer babies, the share of boys swings further from half, so passing 60% is more common (about 15% of days with 15 births vs about 7% with 45).

changed.what: Slider moves in steps of 5 babies
changed.why: With other sizes the '60%' cut-off falls between whole numbers and the chance zig-zags (e.g. 6 babies beats 5), which would muddy the trend.

math_check: Exact binomial: P(at least 10 boys of 15) = 0.151 (about 55 days/year); P(at least 28 of 45) = 0.068 (about 25 days). Simulated runs gave 52 vs 29 and 59 vs 26. For sizes 5 to 45 in steps of 5 the expected days fall steadily (68, 63, 55, 48, 42, 37, 32, 28, 25). In a walkthrough the dark squares counted from the SVG equalled the readouts (61+28=89, 62+17=79). The over-60% test uses whole numbers (boys*5 > babies*3).
